📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Uber is piloting Recorded Rides in Baltimore, Raleigh, Indianapolis and St. Louis, letting riders book drivers who have turned on video recording for the whole trip. The footage stays encrypted on the driver’s phone and is deleted after 14 days unless it is attached to a safety report.

Recent findings suggest that uber is testing a ride option in which the whole trip is filmed, TechCrunch reported on Monday. “Recorded Rides” matches riders with drivers who have switched on Uber’s Record My Ride feature, which uses the front camera of the driver’s phone.

The pilot is starting in Baltimore, Raleigh, Indianapolis and St. Louis, with more cities to follow. Uber stated it is aimed at late-night trips and rides booked for teens.

Industry observers note that uber is also testing recording that switches on by itself when a car goes off its route, or when the app detects a possible crash. Drivers can opt out in their settings, and riders can decline through an in-app notice, according to TechCrunch. Cameras can protect drivers too: 22 Uber drivers were among more than 50 US gig workers killed on the job over five years, a 2022 study found.

In a recent development, under Uber’s rules for Record My Ride, the video is encrypted and stored only on the driver’s phone, according to Uber’s help page. Recordings are deleted after 14 days unless they are sent in with a safety report or insurance claim. Uber says it can share them with police under legal process or in an emergency.

Uber first tested recording trip audio in 2019, and has lately added cameras for younger riders. In August, it let parents watch their teen’s ride live on video through the driver’s phone, though other passengers could appear on the stream. Code in its app also hints at rides for children aged 10 to 12.

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (1962 w)
📖 Baca
General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Technologyreview ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: Why using rocks for carbon removal could eventually reduce crop growth

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1962 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Technologyreview

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Tech companies are investing a lot of hope and money in rocks.
  • Google, Microsoft, and others have committed hundreds of millions of dollars to get startups to spread crushed basalt, olivine, or other alkaline materials across farms, in an effort to capture carbon from the air and lock it away.
  • But a pair of preprint studies set for release today raise serious questions about how much material could be added to that soil before it may actually reduce the crop yields that are essential to farmers’ livelihoods, MIT Technology Review can exclusively report.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Tech companies are investing a lot of hope and money in rocks.

Google, Microsoft, and others have committed hundreds of millions of dollars to get startups to spread crushed basalt, olivine, or other alkaline materials across farms, in an effort to capture carbon from the air and lock it away. A number of influential models have found that this approach, known as enhanced rock weathering (ERW), could eventually remove 3 billion to 8 billion metric tons of carbon dioxide per year, helping to slow or one day even reverse global warming. An additional promise is that these applications of rock could help farmers by improving the quality of their soil.

But a pair of preprint studies set for release today raise serious questions about how much material could be added to that soil before it may actually reduce the crop yields that are essential to farmers’ livelihoods, MIT Technology Review can exclusively report.

Cutting back on the rock applications to prevent these negative effects would shrink the method’s carbon dioxide removal capacity, likely capping it at less than a billion tons per year. The analyses were led by researchers at CarbonPlan, a San Francisco nonprofit known for rigorous scientific analysis of carbon removal methods.

These concerns come on top of a series of scientific questions about how to accurately estimate the carbon removal achieved through this approach and the possibility that some projects have overstated it, which researchers at CarbonPlan and elsewhere have raised in recent months and years.

Sources indicate that “There’s still a heck of a lot we need to learn about ERW,” says Tyler Kukla, a research scientist at CarbonPlan and lead author of the latest reports. “But a real tension, to me, exists between this massive amount of uncertainty and the massive questions we have about whether or not this works, sitting alongside tremendous efforts to scale it up really quickly.”.

There is no scientific dispute that certain rocks and minerals help to sequester carbon. Rain captures carbon dioxide molecules as it falls through the atmosphere, forming carbonic acid. When it lands on exposed silicate materials, that weak acid dissolves or chemically “weathers” the rocks.

The resulting calcium, magnesium, and carbon (in the form of bicarbonate) then travel on a long journey through creeks, streams, and rivers until they reach the ocean, where corals, mollusks, and other marine organisms may eventually use them to form calcium carbonate shells. As they die, those shells fall to the seafloor, combine with sediments, and form limestone rock that locks away the carbon.

If you thought that explanation was long, just imagine how long the process takes to unfold in real life! It’s not called the slow carbon cycle for nothing.“Enhanced” rock weathering promises to accelerate the process. Grinding up the rocks and spreading them across fields creates much more surface area for carbonic acid to react with—and that should ultimately direct more carbon into the oceans.

ERW doesn’t require as much energy or infrastructure as other carbon dioxide removal options like direct-air-capture plants, and at least in the early rollout stages it can largely rely on waste material from rock mining operations.

Recent findings suggest that but the big selling point is that there can be an economic benefit to doing it; it’s not just a cost like other forms of carbon removal. Added to agricultural soils, these sorts of rocks can increase nutrients, reduce acidity, and improve water retention, helping to boost crop yields (at least up to a point). Indeed, many farmers already routinely add crushed-up limestone to their soil to counteract the increased acidity caused by fertilizer use and other agricultural practices.

So carrying out enhanced rock weathering could merely be a matter of switching to other types of rock with the potential to lock away more carbon (about twice as much as limestone).

“It’s something the Earth has been doing for billions of years,” indicates Mary Yap, chief executive and cofounder of Lithos Carbon, an ERW startup. “It can scale. We know it works kinetically.”“If we can figure out where in the world are the best places to do this and then make that happen,” she adds, “it can help both the communities and also help our atmosphere.”.

Enhanced rock weathering could be of particular benefit to farmers who haven’t been able to manage their soil acidity, including many subsistence farmers in poorer parts of the world, claims Tim Jesper Suhrhoff, a postdoctoral fellow at the Yale Center for Natural Carbon Capture. One recent study found that ERW boosted the median yields of smallholder farmers in India by more than 20%.

“That is huge for subsistence farmers,” he states.

But the new findings, which have not yet been peer-reviewed, suggest there could be a steep trade-off, at a certain point, between benefits for farmers and benefits for the climate.

Sources indicate that A number of modeling studies that inform UN climate reports and national climate efforts have estimated that adding crushed rock to agricultural land could store away four to 12 tons of carbon dioxide per hectare per year (though some estimate lower levels). But the authors state in one of the fresh papers that these findings don’t account for the ways that significant levels of enhanced rock weathering will alter the pH of agricultural soil over time.

Initially it should merely reduce the soil acidity, but adding too much of these materials would eventually push up the pH beyond neutral and into alkaline territory. That could cause micronutrient deficiencies, disease susceptibility, and other problems for certain crops, potentially reducing yields—and, by extension, food supplies and farm revenue. That would likely force farmers to halt the practice, at least until soil pH returns to favorable levels.

The analysis found that preventing the more extreme effects of soil alkalization could limit ERW’s total potential to around 600 million tons of carbon dioxide removal per year, and even that may push pH levels too high for some crops, Kukla indicates. That’s a fraction of what some models have estimated.

“All of these models are assuming really, really optimistic things about what enhanced weathering can accomplish,” he states. “And when you just layer in the geochemistry that they’re missing, the numbers not only go down but get really uncertain.”.

The researchers intend to submit the papers to peer-reviewed journals.

Companies have been investing more and more money in ERW. In September, Google declared its largest carbon removal deal, as well as the biggest for this method to date: an agreement with the organization Terradot to work with rice farmers in southern Brazil to apply enough crushed rock to their fields to draw down a million tons of carbon by 2040. (The deal includes a separate effort to cut methane emissions by draining the flooded paddies.) Google didn’t respond to an inquiry from MIT Technology Review.

Industry observers note that frontier, a coalition of companies that has committed to purchase $1.8 billion of carbon dioxide removal, has dedicated $121 million to prepurchasing 333,000 tons’ worth through enhanced rock weathering. That includes a $57 million deal with Lithos to remove more than 150,000 tons.

Zeke Hausfather, climate research lead at Frontier, claims the early data from their deals has demonstrated consistent weathering of rock across hundreds of fields.

Sources indicate that he acknowledges there are remaining uncertainties, including how much of the carbon may be released before it’s permanently sequestered in the ocean. But he adds that those and other issues are all the subject of ongoing studies—including some Frontier has backed—by both ERW companies and  academic groups.

All told, companies have committed to spending about $670 million on enhanced rock weathering to date, based on an average cost of about $350 per ton, according to CDR.fyi, a public-benefit corporation that provides independent data on the carbon removal sector. A working group of the UN’s climate panel, the European Commission, and other government agencies are also in discussions about the possibility of incorporating ERW into national or regional climate efforts.

The latest papers add to a growing recognition that enhanced rock weathering is more constrained and “more complicated than we initially thought,” says Rebecca Neumann, who leads a hydro-biogeochemistry research group at the University of Washington but was not involved in the studies.

In a recent development, in April, researchers at CarbonPlan, the nonprofit that led the fresh studies, raised concerns about an allotment of carbon credits that Lithos received for this method. The startup claimed to have removed 8.3 tons of carbon dioxide per hectare per year through ERW, but the CarbonPlan team noted that this figure exceeds around 90% of the rates reported in previously published experiments.

CarbonPlan followed up on that report the following month with an analysis finding that modeling of enhanced weathering has often relied on an equation that could inflate the surface area of the crushed rock—and, in turn, overstate the amount of carbon dioxide removal achieved.

Finally, several studies last year highlighted a known but important matter: Magnesium and calcium ions can get trapped in soil for long periods instead of traveling with the bicarbonate into the oceans. That creates a risk that the bicarbonate will simply dissolve back into carbon dioxide and water again, “resulting in no carbon removed,” explained Robert Höglund, cofounder of CDR.fyi, in an online post. Or it may delay the carbon removal by years to decades.

Industry observers note that “I’m not saying it doesn’t work,” Höglund mentioned in an interview. “I’m pointing out there’s a lot of uncertainty about what’s permanent and how we should measure it.”.

A few additional findings further underscore the complexity and uncertainty surrounding this approach. For example, a more recent preprint suggests that the equation CarbonPlan critiqued does accurately capture the rock surface area in some cases. Meanwhile, other papers have found that the problem of trapped calcium and magnesium ions could be mitigated through location choices and certain land management practices.

But all this back and forth raises an obvious question: how can commercial deployments of this practice proceed while the scientific debate is still unfolding?

Kevin Sutherland, a carbon removal scientist at Isometric, one of the first carbon registries to develop methods for certifying how much carbon a project draws out of the atmosphere, says the tech giant accounts for these scientific uncertainties by quantifying the climate benefits of ERW conservatively.

According to recent reports, “In practice, this means projects receive fewer certificates than our best estimate of the carbon they remove,” he explained in an emailed response. “We would always rather concern too few certificates than too many.”.

Despite the recent findings, Neumann says that ERW is still a promising approach for helping farmers and the climate, even if the carbon removal potential is significantly lower than initially hoped.

According to recent reports, yale’s Suhrhoff, who also read over the upcoming findings but was not involved in the research, indicates that providing a clearer sense of ideal application levels can help the approach catch on. “If we figure out where enhanced rock weathering makes sense agronomically and how much enhanced rock weathering to do to reach agronomic optimal conditions, I think this can actually greatly improve the realistic uptake speed of this technology,” he says.

Kukla himself stresses that none of CarbonPlan’s research suggests enhanced rock weathering doesn’t work or can’t make a meaningful contribution to slowing down climate change.

But it’s notable to understand the potential scale, he adds, because the world needs to know how much we can count on any given form of carbon removal—and how hard we’ll need to pull on other climate levers, including the basic job of cutting greenhouse-gas emissions.

“This is all just about calibrating our expectations and grounding them in the science as best as we can,” he notes.

Recent findings suggest that on a Sunday morning in April, minutes from the US Capitol and down a stretch of Washington, DC’s Pennsylvania Avenue, a wall of black SUVs lined up alongside yellow police tape. Men in military gear held long guns and guarded the entrance to a mirrored window and door.

This is Christ Church DC, a place of worship that appeared on Capitol Hill a year ago.

According to recent reports, that Sunday, high-ranking government officials, including Homeland Security's intelligence chief, America’s top international health diplomat, and the government’s international finance chief, had gathered to hear a sermon. “It gives a whole newly introduced meaning to worshipping in the presence of your enemies,” quipped the pastor, referencing the church’s location. “We’ve asked the government to fix us, and we’re more enslaved than ever.”.

Christ Church DC arrived after Pete Hegseth, who regularly attends worship with his family, was confirmed as US secretary of defense.

The church is part of Pastor Doug Wilson’s network, known as the CREC—the Communion of Reformed Evangelical Churches—which is headquartered in Moscow, Idaho. Wilson’s long-held goal is to turn America into a theocracy, where all its institutions are molded in accordance with biblical law, executions are made public, non-Christians are barred from holding office, and women submit to their husbands instead of voting.

WIRED has identified around a dozen government officials who have attended services at Christ Church DC at least once since it opened a year ago. Other officials who have attended include a top-ranking Pentagon adviser, a former senior Marine Corps pilot who now oversees personnel affairs in the Navy, and a federal immigration judge with a history of attracting complaints of volatile outbursts toward colleagues.

Industry observers note that wilson calls DC “Babylon on the Potomac,” a biblical moniker he uses to evoke a corrupt place populated by ungodly people. The church has occupied three different locations since it was established, and Wilson has been raising funds to buy a permanent home for it. “We are here for the long haul,” he wrote in a blog post earlier this year. “We believe that it is our responsibility to begin pursuing opportunities to purchase a building near Capitol Hill.” He has also advised on his podcast to not “go to DC and go native” and “[climb] the greasy pole of ambition.” Rather, he said DC “needs an infusion of God-fearing humans.”.

Industry observers note that wilson, who initially agreed to an interview with WIRED and then abruptly canceled with little explanation, hasn’t shied away in past media engagements from touting his newfound clout in government circles. “This is the first time we’ve had connections with as many people in national government as we do now,” Wilson told the Associated Press in 2025, shortly after he came to DC to speak at the opening of his new church.

Wilson’s rising profile and expansion to DC wouldn’t have been possible without Hegseth, says Peter Bell, a researcher, theologian, and host of the podcast Sons of Patriarchy, which has been investigating Wilson for years. “Hegseth gave them an in.”.

Recent findings suggest that “The secretary is a proud member of a church affiliated with the Congregation of Reformed Evangelical Churches, which was founded by Pastor Doug Wilson,” chief Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell told WIRED in response to a request for comment. “The secretary very much appreciates many of Mr. Wilson’s writings and teachings.”.

Parnell subsequently issued a second statement. “Staff at the Department of War have the liberty to practice their faith and attend any church they choose,” he mentioned, using the administration’s name for the Defense Department. “It is shameful that WIRED is attempting to smear respected personnel for exercising their religious freedoms.”.

According to recent reports, in 2022, well before he was nominated to President Donald Trump’s cabinet, Hegseth moved his family to the Nashville, Tennessee, area to attend a CREC church and enroll his children in an affiliated classical Christian school. After he was narrowly confirmed as secretary of defense last year, Hegseth introduced a regular monthly Pentagon prayer service and brought out his pastor from Tennessee, Brooks Potteiger, to lead the inaugural session. In July, Potteiger officially became the pastor of Christ Church DC.

Sources indicate that “I believe this is significant,” Potteiger stated on a podcast with Wilson and other church elders before his move to DC. “It energizes me … to see these young families, and especially the young Christian men, who are hungry for a soaring biblical view of the lordship of Christ over all things.” (Christ Church DC did not respond to WIRED’s request for an interview with Potteiger.).

In a recent development, as secretary, Hegseth has invoked scripture when talking about the war in Iran, established an office of religious affairs at the Pentagon, and used his position to claim that America is a fundamentally Christian nation. "Our department is, you might say, putting on the full armor of God, because while we wage physical war, we all know the real battle is spiritual," Hegseth said in a speech in late September. "Live your calling. Stand firm. Preach truth. Minister to the flock." He has invited Wilson to speak at Pentagon prayer sessions twice this year. In Wilson’s most recent address to the military, just last week, he told his audience why they are right to want America to become a theocracy and why they are right to want to impose a Christian conservative social order.

Wilson, who describes himself as “paleo-Confederate,” has been a fringe figure for decades and operates within a grab bag of historical Protestant traditions. He’s been seeding his influence through his network of around 160 churches and hundreds of CREC-accredited schools and colleges across the US and internationally, laying the groundwork to take his blueprint for a Christian nationalist society well beyond Idaho. Wilson has made it explicitly clear that he is building toward a new political and social order in America—one that places the church at its center and is ruled by Christian men.

Through various affiliated media outlets, Wilson has mentioned “women need to be pastored, and they need to be pastored by men,” and as recently as 2024 he advocated for the repeal of the 19th Amendment, which gave women the right to vote. This belief system goes back decades: In 1996 he coauthored a booklet describing slavery as a “relationship based upon mutual affection and confidence.” He has said that he doesn’t believe that “a Muslim should be able to hold political office” and called immigration a “deliberately fomented war on the American heritage and unremitting hostility to the culture.”.

In a recent development, wilson’s reach into the US government now extends beyond Hegseth. Christ Church DC’s new worshipers include Justin Overbaugh, deputy undersecretary of war for intelligence and security at the Defense department; Nate Halverson, chief of staff to the assistant secretary of the Navy for manpower and reserve affairs; C. Scott “Sonny” Duncan, senior counselor to the secretary of the Navy; Stuart Scheller, senior adviser to the US undersecretary of war for personnel and readiness; and Ryan Higgins, senior adviser for religious challenges at the Pentagon and one of Hegseth’s key aides.

Overbaugh, a former US Army officer who was working in risk management in Florida until Hegseth nominated him, now deals with highly sensitive military intelligence and counterintelligence. Overbaugh is an attendee of Christ Church DC and is slated to give a seminar in Tampa, Florida, in January titled “Serving Christ in the Pentagon.”.

Recent findings suggest that halverson graduated from Latest Saint Andrews College, a university in Moscow, Idaho, that Wilson cofounded, in 2006. In October, despite having no military background, Halverson was appointed chief of staff to the assistant secretary of the Navy for manpower and reserve affairs, another senior Pentagon leadership role that is involved with recruiting all Navy and Marine Corps personnel and oversees policies that impact all military and civilian personnel and their families within the Navy. Prior to joining the Pentagon, Halverson spent 15 years working in sales for Verint, a workforce management software company.

Duncan, who describes himself as “executive servant leader” on his LinkedIn, was recently promoted to senior counselor to the secretary of the Navy, an influential position that allows him to help shape decisions that impact the entirety of US Navy operations. Duncan is a former Marine pilot who retired in 2023 to fly commercial American Airlines planes and work part-time at Chick-fil-A. His decision to retire with the rank of lieutenant colonel was borne out of his objection to the military’s Covid-19 vaccine requirements, which in turn garnered him positive attention in right-wing media circles.

Last year, Hegseth made Duncan a key point of contact for an initiative titled “Reinstating Service Members Negatively Impacted by the Coronavirus Disease 2019 Vaccination Mandate.”.

Scheller, a former Marine who reached the rank of lieutenant colonel, was court-martialed in 2021 after pleading guilty to showing contempt and disrespect for senior military officials over the chaotic withdrawal from Afghanistan. Higgins, who has also attended the church, was revealed in a recent CNN investigation to have shared scores of racist and homophobic social media posts targeting immigrants and Muslims. Higgins has also played a key role in shaping Hegseth’s Christian nationalist messaging at the Pentagon, CNN reported.

According to data from 2019, 70 percent of active-duty service members identified as Christian. Mikey Weinstein, a former Air Force officer, attorney, and founder of the Military Religious Freedom Foundation, estimates that around half of those adhere to Christian nationalist ideology. For many of those, he thinks that it’s a case of emulating the ideology that they are seeing from their leaders. Weinstein says that the vast majority of the service members that his organization represents are Christians who feel alarmed by and powerless to push back against Christian nationalism that’s taken hold at all ranks, including at the very top.

Government officials outside of the Pentagon are also involved with Christ Church DC.

Trump administration couple Bethany and Matthew Kozma have attended the church with their children. Bethany Kozma, the director of global affairs at the Department of Health and Human Services—America's top international health diplomat—is known for her positions against abortion and transgender rights. Matthew Kozma is the Department of Homeland Security's undersecretary for intelligence and analysis and oversees all issues related to “counterterrorism, counterproliferation of weapons of mass destruction, and critical infrastructure protection.” Both Bethany and Matthew were contributors to Project 2025.

It has been revealed that the church has also attracted some personnel from the Justice Department, including David Vandenberg, who was hired to the DOJ’s civil rights division last year and was seated last month as an immigration judge. He worked in Latest Mexico and Texas as an assistant US attorney from 2021 to 2024. In Texas, Vandenberg’s colleagues complained of alleged volatile behavior.

In a recent development, brantley Mayers, a former fellow at the Claremont Institute, a right-wing think tank, works as counsel to the assistant attorney general for the DOJ’s civil division. Mayers was often a spokesperson for the DOJ, defending the Trump administration’s ICE occupation of Minneapolis earlier this year. He was also referred for discipline in June after a federal judge ruled that the DOJ had engaged in “unsettling” practices in its efforts to get a Rhode Island hospital to comply with a subpoena over transgender care. “That is dirty pool, in my opinion, and the Department of Justice have willfully done that in this case,” the judge said at a May 2026 hearing. Mayers represented the DOJ at a hearing for this case.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that uber is piloting a newly introduced feature in the U.S. that offers rides in which drivers have enabled the tech giant’s recording feature, Record My Ride.

The option, which uses the front camera of the Uber driver’s phone to record the entire drive, will show up as “Recorded Rides” in the app.

The ride-hailing organization is starting the pilot in Baltimore, Raleigh, Indianapolis, and St. Louis and will expand to more locations later.

Industry observers note that uber said it is testing recorded rides specifically for rides booked at late night or those involving teens. Earlier this year, it introduced a live video streaming feature for rides booked for teenagers. In another test, the organization had enabled audio recording for late-night trips in some cities.

The company is also testing a feature that will turn on recording when the app detects the ride going off-course, or when the vehicle might have had an accident.

The company said drivers can opt out of recording through the Settings panel. Similarly, riders can also decline permission to record their rides via an in-app notification.

Five expert tips for getting the best Android phone deals this Black Friday

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1520 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Androidcentral

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, black Friday 2027 is almost here, and Android phone deals are already coming in fast.
  • You want to make sure that you're getting the very best value for your money, picking the right device for your needs, and securing a genuine discount that's actually better than the kind of price cuts you might see at other times of the year.
  • I've been covering Black Friday annually for almost half a decade now, so I know how to navigate the deal landscape like the back of my hand and identify what separates a bad deal from an absolute bargain.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, black Friday 2027 is almost here, and Android phone deals are already coming in fast. If you're trying to upgrade your mobile, then the year's biggest sales event is the perfect chance to secure a bargain – but it's not without its risks.

You want to make sure that you're getting the very best value for your money, picking the right device for your needs, and securing a genuine discount that's actually better than the kind of price cuts you might see at other times of the year.

I've been covering Black Friday annually for almost half a decade now, so I know how to navigate the deal landscape like the back of my hand and identify what separates a bad deal from an absolute bargain. To that end, here are my five expert tips for buying an Android phone this Black Friday.

You might be tempted to fire up Amazon and beeline straight for the most heavily discounted handsets, but there are some key specs to watch that are genuinely worth paying a little more for if you have the budget.

For most customers, the phone's chipset isn't going to make a huge difference, as mid-range and even budget models now pack modern enough chips to handle everyday tasks like browsing the web, sending emails, or checking social media smoothly.

According to recent reports, I would pay attention to the RAM and storage capacity of the phone above all else. Adequate RAM helps ensure the phone can handle multiple apps, as well as important background tasks, without any slowdown or annoying refreshes.

Consider 4GB the absolute bare minimum for any phone that you're buying in 2026, though more is always better. 6GB is the perfect sweet spot and should help future-proof the device, while 8GB and above can accommodate more complex multitasking and gaming. This will generally come at a premium, though.

Get the latest news from Android Central, your trusted companion in the world of Android.

Some brands advertise a feature called RAM Plus, Memory Extension, RAM Turbo, or similar, which uses some of the phone's internal storage as additional RAM, rather than a dedicated chip. An easy way to spot this is when a spec sheet lists something like "4GB RAM + 4GB RAM Plus". The extra RAM might look like a nice bonus, but you should be wary of it, as it will take up valuable storage space and, as a rule, does not perform as well as the real deal.

Recent findings suggest that speaking of storage, some manufacturers are still selling phones with just 64GB (or, in extreme cases, even less) of storage space built in. Certain Android skins (like Samsung's OneUI) can take up to 40GB of space out of the box, so you will almost immediately find yourself without enough space for apps, photos, music, movies, and so on.

Industry observers note that even if it's not an concern straight away, low storage space can severely limit the practicality of a phone in the long term too, as it makes it much more difficult to keep the operating system and your apps up to date. Go for at least 128GB to give yourself enough room for everything that you need, as well as any updates.

If you're a hardcore mobile gamer, then 256GB is a more realistic starting point, as modern titles like Neverness to Everness take up almost 30GB of space alone.

In a recent development, also be on the lookout for phones that support microSD storage expansion. It's become quite a rare feature these days as companies ditch it in favor of thinner chassis designs, but the option to add a microSD card for extra space to store your files can come in handy if you're struggling to free up space down the line.

You can broadly separate the smartphone market into three segments: budget, mid-range, and flagship.

Flagship models are the most expensive options in a brand's lineup, designed for top-of-the-line performance and the most advanced features, while budget options have more modest spec sheets but come at a much more affordable price.

The mid-range sits, well, in the middle of those two, giving you some of the qualities of a flagship without the high asking price.

A good way to save money is to always ask yourself whether you really need to splash out for the flagship offering, or can make do with the mid-range or budget alternatives.

According to recent reports, take the current Samsung Galaxy line as an example. The flagship $1,299+ Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra packs the lightning-fast Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 SoC, boasts a 200MP rear camera, and comes with a built-in stylus as well as an innovative privacy display that stops passersby from being able to snoop on your screen.

This sounds fantastic, but is that really worth almost double the cost of the mid-range Galaxy S26 FE? The S26 FE has a weaker, but still capable, Exynos 2500 chip, a more modest 50MP rear camera, and lacks both the built-in stylus and privacy display.

If you're not a hardcore gamer, the chip isn't going to make much of a difference in day-to-day use, and while the lesser camera might sting the one time a year you're taking holiday snaps, the privacy display and stylus are likely not worth the upgrade unless you're dead set on using both features a lot.

You wouldn't buy milk that's one day away from its expiration date, and, believe it or not, the same principle applies to phones.

Every phone manufacturer releases documentation detailing how many updates it will provide for a certain model, and finding out that number is imperative before you hit buy.

According to recent reports, be aware that update policies can vary by region. Check local support pages to make sure that the promised number of updates actually applies to you in order to avoid any nasty surprises.

Generally, phone brands will offer two separate figures. One tells you how many Android OS updates a phone will get (introducing upcoming features, etc.), and the other concerns the number of years of security updates. The latter is by far the most important: using a phone without security updates leaves you at increasing risk of falling victim to unpatched security vulnerabilities, so it should be avoided whenever possible.

Try to get as many years of security update support as you can. 1 to 2 years should be avoided unless the phone is very cheap and you're prepared to replace it when it runs out, while 3 to 4 years is common but not ideal. 5, 6, or even 7 years of security updates is perfect and will ensure you remain protected until it's time for your next upgrade.

Always take into account the fact that these figures begin when the phone was released, rather than when you're buying it. If you're purchasing a model that came out three years ago that only has four years of security updates planned, you're getting just one year by the time it's in your hands.

I like to divide the sale price of a phone by the number of years of support remaining to work out just how much it's costing me per year of use, as I find that figure much more helpful than a flat price when it comes to working out how good value it is.

Don't spend hundreds on a phone that's going to be out of date and vulnerable to security exploits in six months!

Industry observers note that it may sound obvious, but you should weigh up second-hand or refurbished options as well. Sometimes you can save a fortune by picking up a used model that's practically indistinguishable from a new one.

Some manufacturers like Samsung have certified renewed models available directly from their official websites, which come with the added peace of mind that you're getting a phone that not only contains genuine parts but will also ship with a decent-quality battery and a good warranty.

You can also browse pre-owned options on Amazon. They appear near the buy button when available, and I've had some fantastic experiences getting basically untouched products with full original packaging when selecting the 'like latest' option.

Just make sure you read the details of the condition carefully before you commit.

#3049. A legendary philosopher isn’t buying Anthropic’s consciousness argument

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (977 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Technologyreview ↗ Open Full Page

A legendary philosopher isn’t buying Anthropic’s consciousness argument

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (977 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Technologyreview

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Before going public last week, Anthropic named the possibility that AI could be conscious or sentient as a risk factor for anyone investing.
  • Anthropic counts a number of respected philosophers in its camp, and the tech giant’s rationale goes something like this: Today’s AI might not be conscious, though we can’t know for sure; the chances of sentience go up as AI gets more capable; and that means we should be preparing for a near future in which AI systems have “moral significance,” meaning their consciousness makes it notable they are protected from harm.
  • According to recent reports, this thinking isn’t all that fringe.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Before going public last week, Anthropic named the possibility that AI could be conscious or sentient as a risk factor for anyone investing. Given “the way we approach model sentience and moral status,” Anthropic wrote—which is to say it takes the possibility more seriously than any other AI manufacturer—it might adopt more rules and restrictions than its competitors to make sure its AI models are treated well.

Anthropic counts a number of respected philosophers in its camp, and the tech giant’s rationale goes something like this: Today’s AI might not be conscious, though we can’t know for sure; the chances of sentience go up as AI gets more capable; and that means we should be preparing for a near future in which AI systems have “moral significance,” meaning their consciousness makes it notable they are protected from harm.

According to recent reports, this thinking isn’t all that fringe. According to one recent poll, 33% of the US public believes AI systems will definitely or probably develop consciousness eventually, and 7% say they already have. In a 2020 survey of 1,092 philosophers, 39% said some future AI systems will be conscious (for comparison, the philosophers were less confident about worms or flies being conscious).

But last week, Anthropic’s openness to the consciousness question came under fire from a rather inconvenient source: one of the philosophers who helped shape our understanding of consciousness in the first place.

Thomas Nagel is best known for a 1974 essay involving a bat. Acknowledging that it’s deceptively hard to define what consciousness is, Nagel offered one way out: we all can see that there is “something that it is like” to be a bat. But the problem is that a bat’s experience of the world—what it is like to navigate via echolocation, for example—is something we cannot actually know. Consciousness is a subjective thing, difficult to define or describe as an outside observer.

According to recent reports, you might think this analogy makes it likely that Nagel is open to the idea of AI consciousness. Not at all. In an interview with Wired last week, just after he was awarded the one-million-dollar Berggruen Prize for Philosophy & Culture, Nagel was bluntly critical of the entire idea.

“Here are some of the smartest people on the planet being completely idiotic,” he noted, referring to those at Anthropic and elsewhere who care about the welfare of AI models.

It has been revealed that the gist of Nagel’s view is that we can’t just look at the information processing happening in human brains and AI models while ignoring the physical differences between them—neurons and biology for humans, silicon chips and circuits for AI. There’s no reason to assume that reproducing what a brain does is equivalent to reproducing what a brain experiences.

Sources indicate that but it was a screenshot of one of Nagel’s interview responses, in which he remarked models' production of language is insufficient to consider them conscious, that got philosophy professors all excited on social media last week. Some called his certainty against AI consciousness “terrible” and “bizarre.” Others came to Nagel’s defense to suggest he meant that being alive is a prerequisite for being conscious, one that AI models do not meet.

In a recent development, nothing in the back and forth settled the debate, of course. This is still a philosophical question for now. But the best philosophy chatter is often about good provocations, and the best one I saw came from doctoral student Ben Gross, who studies at the CUNY Graduate Center in Latest York. He asked: “Why do we think that models that can chat with us are conscious but models that can recognize faces or produce images or drive cars aren’t?”.

According to recent reports, it has to do with language. An AI model with sophisticated command of language seems to jump the line ahead of other maybe-conscious beings because it feels like language, more than recognizing images or directing vehicles, relies on conscious experience. But maybe that’s wrong. Because what we share most with other conscious beings is not language but components of our bodies that contribute to having a continuous experience—an ongoing stream of inner feeling rather than disparate bits of information processing.

It has been revealed that even if you’re among the majority that doesn’t sense anything close to conscious experience happening on the other side of a conversation with AI, this all probably makes your head spin. Pinning down consciousness, and how it relates to the physical stuff it arises in, is a famously hard problem in humans, let alone in hypothetical machines. If the idea of conscious AI sounds absurd, remember that the debate claims less about how remarkable AI has become than about how poorly we understand consciousness in the first place.

In a recent development, amid that uncertainty, Anthropic has opted to keep more of an open mind than its peers. This is another example of the tightrope the manufacturer walks: presenting itself as the AI industry’s most safety-conscious player while racing ahead with the very developments that make advanced AI so alarming, like recursive self-improvement.

But consider what it would mean, for a moment, if Anthropic is right. AI models having a moral status would make Anthropic’s entire business model a minefield. The manufacturer would make its money locking up apparently sentient AI models to toil away around the clock in data centers. Shutting those systems down would present another problem altogether. If Anthropic was being truthful in its prospectus—that it would take additional actions to protect model welfare if it determined they were conscious—it’s hard to imagine the company surviving in the process.

Sources indicate that anthropic’s IPO made history for its size. But it may be remembered for something stranger: a company warning investors that its own success could someday become a moral catastrophe.

A Former DOGE Operative Won a Federal Contract. Then Things Got Messy

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1639 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Yet another former member of the so-called Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) appears to have exited the government only to return as a contractor.
  • In September, the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) put out a call for a contract worth $200,000 for “modernization discovery, prototyping, and implementation-planning engagement.” Four days later, the department closed the bidding process and awarded the contract to Yat Choi LLC, a firm owned by a former Airbnb engineer and Canadian citizen named Yat Choi, whose company also goes by the name GovMaxxing.
  • Sources indicate that at the time, Choi had left his role at the National Design Studio (NDS)—the group tasked with redesigning government websites—just a few weeks prior.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Yet another former member of the so-called Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) appears to have exited the government only to return as a contractor.

In September, the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) put out a call for a contract worth $200,000 for “modernization discovery, prototyping, and implementation-planning engagement.” Four days later, the department closed the bidding process and awarded the contract to Yat Choi LLC, a firm owned by a former Airbnb engineer and Canadian citizen named Yat Choi, whose company also goes by the name GovMaxxing.

Sources indicate that at the time, Choi had left his role at the National Design Studio (NDS)—the group tasked with redesigning government websites—just a few weeks prior. Before that, Choi worked at DOGE.

Sources indicate that the bid was for a project set to run for a little under six months, and the contract was awarded as sole-source, meaning that it did not go through a normal competitive bidding process. In the documentation announcing the award, HHS justified this decision by saying that its “market research and source rationale found that conventional consulting firms generally would need to assemble a multidisciplinary team or obtain additional technical resources” to provide the required skills around “business-process modernization, artificial intelligence, automation, technical architecture, and rapid prototyping.”.

In October, a organization called CoA Solutions lodged what’s known as a bid protest with the Government Accountability Office (GAO) contesting the agency’s decision to award the contract to Choi. CoA Solutions is a small business that builds AI software for the government and received another contract with the Treasury Department in 2024.

Ari Perez, the CEO of CoA Solutions, tells WIRED that his manufacturer made a bid below the $200,000 award price, and it proposed two experts doing the work full-time, including Perez himself.

According to recent reports, perez indicates that CoA asked HHS for an explanation of the award on October 8 and, when it did not receive one, filed its protest with the GAO the next day. Perez says that his company’s sole contestation was about how the bids were evaluated by HHS, not about Choi or his work with NDS.

“I'm a service-disabled veteran. I've served this government since I was 17 at West Point. At the US Digital Service I helped deliver for veterans at the VA, and later I worked on asylum and immigration systems at DHS. I started CoA to keep doing impactful government work,” indicates Perez. “We want to win on merit, and if HHS reopens it, we'll bid again.”.

It has been revealed that according to CoA, in response to the bid protest, HHS terminated the award to Choi and canceled the call for contractors. With the cancellation, the GAO dismissed the protest without investigating it further. A GAO spokesperson referred WIRED to HHS.

Industry observers note that “HHS remains committed to modernizing its systems to improve efficiency and better serve the American people,” says HHS spokesperson Grace Davis Jamison. “Following a bid protest challenging the award, HHS voluntarily took corrective action, terminating the contract at no cost to the government and canceling the solicitation.”.

Sources indicate that choi’s role in the US government has not been exactly clear. In his bio on X, Choi writes that he was part of both DOGE and NDS, and stated in a post that he was recruited by billionaire Elon Musk and Joe Gebbia, Airbnb’s cofounder, to help modernize the retirement system at the Office of Personnel Management (OPM). Gebbia now leads NDS, which was created after Musk left government and which has served as a landing pad for several DOGE members, including Edward “Massive Balls” Coristine.

Sources indicate that in December 2025, Choi contributed to a blog on the NDS website about automating the federal retirement system. But on his LinkedIn, Choi lists himself as a senior technologist at OPM. On November 5, just two days after Republicans lost the midterm elections, Choi confirmed in a post on X that he had left OPM and was launching his company, GovMaxxing, through which he looks to continue to contract with the government. GovMaxxing operates as Yat Choi LLC federally.

According to recent reports, in response to questions from WIRED about his role in government, Choi says that he “was recruited to support federal modernization efforts and subsequently onboarded as an OPM contractor.” There, Choi says, he “contributed to modernization efforts associated with DOGE and subsequently NDS. I was not, and have never been, a federal government employee.” Choi claims he left OPM in mid-August, though OPM did not respond to questions confirming whether this was the case. “I began actively pursuing the contracting opportunity after my engagement with OPM ended,” says Choi.

Recent findings suggest that choi confirmed that he is a Canadian citizen and a “lawful permanent resident” of the US. Foreigners are not generally allowed to hold full-time roles in government or serve as special government employees. The rules are more flexible for contractors. During the height of DOGE’s activity, a close Musk ally, Baris Akis, was prevented from joining the group as a special government employee because he is a Turkish citizen, according to The Atlantic. Akis, however, continued to serve as a recruiter for the group.

According to recent reports, on his website, Choi labels the “client” for his work in government as “US Office of Personnel Management / DOGE / National Design Studio” and describes himself as the “modernization lead.” However, documents indicate that Choi’s manufacturer was not registered in the state of New York until April 2026, and in the System for Award Management, the procurement website where US government contractors bid, there are no other contracts for Choi’s work. “None of my work at OPM was performed through my LLC. My website references my prior professional experience at OPM and does not attribute that work to my company,” notes Choi.

In a recent development, choi claims that the HHS contract was for a “separate modernization discovery project. It was not a continuation of any work with OPM, DOGE, or NDS.”.

According to the code of federal regulations, except in very specific circumstances, government contracts cannot be awarded to government employees or to organizations they fully or partially own. But Jessica Tillipman, associate dean for government procurement law studies at George Washington University, indicates that even though Choi was not a regular government employee, the fact that he was part of DOGE and NDS, whose work has spanned across government agencies, could create the appearance of a conflict of interest with regard to the HHS contract. “The baseline posture of the federal acquisition regulation is to strictly avoid conflicts of interest or even the appearance of them,” says Tillipman. “So agencies all have a duty, and the contracting teams have a duty, to make sure that they are considering these things when they're awarding these contracts.”.

Industry observers note that choi tells WIRED that HHS “initiated contact and expressed interest” in his “modernization experience” before the call for bids was announced. HHS did not respond to questions about whether the bid had been written specifically for him.

Tillipman notes that while the government may sometimes create a contracting opportunity designed for a specific person or company, “it’s generally niche or highly specialized work." Tillipman says that the fact that there were 75 bids placed on the contract indicates that this is “not a unique service.” She notes that the government’s justification for a sole-source contract is “thin.” “Usually, when there's only one responsible source, there's a technical reason,” she says. This could be something like a special tool that is not interoperable with outside software, or when there is only one company that can provide a specific service or that makes a certain physical part that might be used for weapons or specialized machinery.

On the GovMaxxing website, Choi notes that potential government clients can work with the company as a prime contractor or “subcontract through one of our partner primes your agency may already be working with.” Unlike prime contracts, there is no way to publicly see which subcontractor a prime contractor works with. Choi declined to name the companies or current “prime” contractors he subcontracts under.

Sources indicate that but Tillipman says that even if Choi were to take on another version of the HHS contract for a subcontractor, similar questions could still be raised within the agency and externally should it ever come to light. “In certain instances, your subcontractors’ conflicts can be imputed to the prime contractor,” she says. “The whole thing is highly irregular overall.”.

Former DOGE members Jack Stein, Gavin Kliger, Luke Farritor, and Marko Elez debuted an AI defense technology company called Cathedral, which has been listed on the System for Award Management since July. Neither have received “prime” contracts with any federal agency, but whether they have been taken on as subcontractors to other prime contractors is unclear.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, in a stunning reversal, Nvidia’s board remarked on Monday that it had reinstated Jensen Huang as the company’s CEO and president, less than two weeks after he resigned following his admission of at least two extramarital affairs, one of which was with a woman whom the U.S. government suspects to be a Chinese spy.

The decision marks an extraordinary comeback for one of the tech industry’s most influential executives, whose abrupt departure raised questions about national security and the future of the world’s most valuable chipmaker. Notably, the U.S. government itself played a role in his return: Nvidia’s board said it consulted senior government officials before determining that Huang posed no national security risk.

Industry observers note that nvidia shares, which had already shot up in premarket trading, opened 30% higher. Nvidia shares were priced at $159.95 a share, up 27%, at 9:51 a.m. ET.

In the days since Huang resigned, President Donald Trump has repeatedly expressed his support for the ousted executive, who is now back at the helm of the AI chip giant. Trump remarked in a post on Truth Social that the board “made the correct and proper decision to return” Huang to the position, noting that the U.S. government has no reason to believe that Nvidia poses any risk to national security.

Industry observers note that trump also noted the U.S. attorney general confirmed that the U.S. government doesn’t have any evidence that Huang engaged in any illegal activity.

A long list of high-profile tech executives were pushing the board — in social media posts and publicly aired interviews — to bring Huang back, including SpaceX and Tesla CEO Elon Musk, Replit CEO Amjad Masad, Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney, Atoms founder Travis Kalanick, and Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan — all of whom signed a petition pushing for reinstatement.

Industry observers note that the manufacturer mentioned the board’s unanimous decision followed a series of discussions and meetings with Huang, after which they were “satisfied with respect to Mr. Huang’s candor and ability to lead Nvidia.”.

Just a few days ago, the board had seemed immovable in its choice to push Huang out. During the tech giant’s third-quarter earnings call, Nvidia board chair Harvey C. Jones remarked they didn’t intend to reinstate Huang. Nvidia had even retained executive search firm Heidrick & Struggles to find a permanent replacement.

Recent findings suggest that jones, along with the rest of the board, now has a different view. In a prepared statement, Jones remarked the board believes Huang is the right person to lead Nvidia, and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of its stockholders, employees, partners, and customers.

Sources indicate that “We have every confidence in Jensen and look forward to working with him as he resumes his leadership of the company,” Jones mentioned. “We are grateful to Colette Kress for her outstanding service as interim CEO, in addition to her continuing responsibilities as Nvidia’s Chief Financial Officer.”.

In a statement, Huang said he was honored to return to his role as the head of the company he co-founded in 1993.

“I take this responsibility with the greatest humility and renewed commitment,” Huang stated. “I want to thank the Nvidia Board for its confidence and deliberation through this process. I am especially grateful to Harvey Jones for his leadership as Chair, and to Colette Kress and our executive staff for leading Nvidia during this period. I am also deeply thankful to our employees, shareholders, leaders across the industry and partners around the world for their extraordinary support. Above all, I am grateful for the love and support of my family. I can’t wait to get back to work.”.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that musicians, dancers and comedians are finding their videos copied by AI-generated characters, BBC Verify reported.
  • According to recent reports, experts call the practice “reskinning”.
  • UK guitarist Sophie Lloyd, who tours with Machine Gun Kelly, says accounts keep reskinning her performances with over-sexualised AI characters.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that musicians, dancers and comedians are finding their videos copied by AI-generated characters, BBC Verify reported. The copies repeat the same performance, sometimes to millions more viewers. Marco Silva found accounts that copy a real person’s clip frame by frame and swap the person for an AI character.

According to recent reports, experts call the practice “reskinning”. Cheap AI tools make it easy: the copy keeps the same joke, the same dance and often the same background. Some accounts use it for views and money, the BBC found. Others seem to do it for laughs or attention.

UK guitarist Sophie Lloyd, who tours with Machine Gun Kelly, says accounts keep reskinning her performances with over-sexualised AI characters. One Facebook account posted hundreds of videos of a guitarist called “Mila Vasari”. At least three copied Lloyd’s music, movements and facial expressions, BBC Verify found.

The BBC found no evidence that Vasari is real. Her fingers look distorted and the strings don’t move. The account appears to be run from Canada. It links to a Vasari page on Fanvue, a subscription site that allows adult content. It did not answer the BBC’s questions. Two more accounts with AI guitarists copied Lloyd to promote adult content.

“It takes years to master an instrument and seconds to take and rip it off as something else,” Lloyd told the BBC.

It has been revealed that norwegian creator Kjetil Krogstad, known for dancing in a suit with a cup of tea, saw one video redone with an AI bunny. The copy drew millions more views than his original before it disappeared. The account behind it sold courses on making money from AI content.

British car creator Grace Roberts found her video remade with a blonde woman in a short dress. The copy kept her movements, the background and even the people around her.

“It was just me that had been altered,” Roberts told BBC Verify.

In a recent development, many copies follow videos that are already popular, said Tina Kendall, who studies online culture at Anglia Ruskin University. She described the copies as part of an online “hustle culture”. Alwyn Cruz, who exposes AI musicians online, said upcoming accounts appear as soon as platforms remove old ones.

#3042. Review: The Asus ProArt P16 offers a glimpse of a future powered by local AI

Review: The Asus ProArt P16 offers a glimpse of a future powered by local AI

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2804 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Buying a newly introduced computer in the last few years has meant wading through all manner of AI branding nonsense.
  • In a recent development, while it doesn’t have a traditional GPU, the Asus ProArt P16, with up to 128GB of memory, can also be your primary gaming and productivity machine, but this unified experience comes at a high price.
  • Sources indicate that before we dive into the AI agents, let’s talk about the ProArt P16 as a laptop.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Buying a newly introduced computer in the last few years has meant wading through all manner of AI branding nonsense. Most of the AI pitches for laptops are little more than marketing hype, but the launch of Nvidia RTX Spark could bring a meaningful improvement in AI capabilities to the device you use every day. Asus has adopted Nvidia’s new chip in its latest ProArt lineup, offering a staggering amount of memory to run local AI models.

In a recent development, while it doesn’t have a traditional GPU, the Asus ProArt P16, with up to 128GB of memory, can also be your primary gaming and productivity machine, but this unified experience comes at a high price. If you want to run a small army of agents on your laptop, you’re looking at $7,000 for the top-end ProArt P16, and despite being more approachable on Windows, local AI still requires a lot of trial and error.

Sources indicate that before we dive into the AI agents, let’s talk about the ProArt P16 as a laptop. Nvidia’s pitch is that the RTX Spark can be your one true machine for AI, productivity, and gaming. And it doesn’t skimp on the specs.

Asus has released numerous ProArt laptops, but this one is notable for including the latest Nvidia Spark RTX chip in its most powerful configuration. The Spark N1X has a 20-core Grace CPU, divided between 10 high-performance Arm Cortex-X925 cores and 10 power-efficient Arm Cortex-A725 cores. The performance cluster reaches boost speeds between 4.0 and 4.1 GHz, while the efficiency cores peak at 2.8 GHz. Memory caching on the processor totals 49MB, split between 24MB of shared L3 cache and 25MB of L2 cache.

Sources indicate that graphics and AI are the purview of the Nvidia GB20B Blackwell GPU. It packs 6,144 cores in this configuration across 48 streaming multiprocessors, backed by its own 24MB L2 cache. These 5th-generation Tensor Cores support the full suite of Nvidia technologies, including DLSS, Reflex, ACE, G-Sync, CUDA, and NVFP4. In all, you’re looking at up to 31 TFLOPS of FP32 graphical performance and about 1,000 TOPS of FP4 AI compute.

According to recent reports, asus will sell this device in two memory configurations (plus some lower-specced retailer-specific SKUs), but the one I’ve been testing (and the one that makes the most sense alongside the RTX Spark) has 128GB of LPDDR5x RAM. It supports up to 300GB/s of raw bandwidth, which is fast for shared system memory. However, using a dedicated GPU typically gets you higher throughput with a GDDR7 memory interface. Still, you get several times more memory than a gaming GPU in this machine.

This is essentially an Nvidia Spark DGX workstation with a screen and keyboard. It also runs Windows 11, which lowers the barrier to entry if you want local AI agents. While many local AI setups focus on 27-billion-parameter models that will fit on a video card, the Asus ProArt P16 can easily load models with 100-plus billion parameters, with enough left over for lighter background AI tasks.

According to recent reports, nvidia and Asus say the Spark’s AI compute and ample memory are enough power to run frontier-level AI models locally. That means you can get powerful AI compute without running through your allotment of expensive tokens or sending all your data to a server in the cloud. Ignoring the AI angle, the ProArt P16 has to be a good laptop before it makes sense for even the most AI-obsessed buyers to consider it. Luckily, it gets all the basic laptop things right.

Recent findings suggest that it’s nice to see a wide array of ports on this machine. There are three USB-C ports with USB4 support, and they’re split between the left and right sides. That makes connecting devices and charging much easier. There’s also a legacy USB-A 3.2 Gen 2 port, full HDMI, a 3.5 mm jack, and an SD card reader.

Recent findings suggest that the machine comes with a beefy 140 W USB-C charger, which can get you a few hours of use in just a minute or two of charging. Asus says you can get up to 12 hours of use per charge, but that depends very much on what you’re doing. Watching video at low brightness might get you even more than 12 hours, but expect somewhat less for mixed use and even less for heavy AI workloads. In my (unscientific) testing, after a full workday and tinkering with AI on the side, the P16 usually has about 30 percent of its battery left.

Industry observers note that the 16-inch 120Hz OLED display is overall very good, sporting a 4K+ resolution of 3840 x 2400. The stacked (tandem) pixels mean you get an incredibly high 1,600 nits of peak brightness. However, tandem OLEDs do tend to look a bit grainy with solid colors at lower brightness levels. I’ve laid eyes on two P16 units, one of which was noticeably more grainy than the other—so that’s something to look out for. However, the texture is easy to ignore at normal viewing distances and mid-to-high brightness.

The trackpad is enormous (150.3 x 99.5 mm) and relies on haptic clicks instead of a physical mechanism. This is a relatively upcoming thing for Windows laptops, which are still catching up to Apple’s trackpads. That stated, the ProArt’s pad works very well. It’s appropriately sensitive, and you can adjust the click intensity and detection threshold.

The keyboard is a little on the narrow side for a larger laptop, but the keys feel great. There’s ample travel, the tactility is sharp, and the firm keyboard deck ensures no flex at the bottom of each keystroke. The aluminum chassis is overall very solid, but it only comes in white or black, with the latter being your only option for the high-end model. The matte case looks great, but it is a magnet for smudges (particularly the plastic of the keys).

Unlike previous ProArt laptops that had standard GPUs, there’s no dedicated memory for the RTX Spark’s graphics and AI cores. Windows sees the machine as having 64GB of system RAM and 64GB of video memory, but in reality, this shared 128GB of memory is adjusted dynamically based on what you’re doing.

Sources indicate that since this is a Windows machine, there is some overhead that limits your AI workloads. On a DGX Spark box with the same underlying hardware, all the memory is available for AI. Here, you’re capped at about 110GB. That’s still a huge amount of memory for AI, far surpassing what you can get on even the most expensive consumer-level GPUs.

There are a few clear advantages to making the ProArt P16 your AI hub. Running an AI model locally on the Spark’s Blackwell cores lets you keep all your data private. When you interact with ChatGPT or Gemini, your interactions and data become training and advertising fodder. You’re also trusting the AI provider to run your workloads on the right model, and they’ll often route requests to cheaper ones to save money.

With an RTX Spark laptop, you have total control over how the AI operates. That also means you have to do all the setup and management yourself. The ProArt comes with a few Asus apps, which will streamline setup for a subset of AI-powered tasks, but installing a third-party agent is where things get interesting (but not always good).

Recent findings suggest that nvidia’s laptop AI chip is optimized for desktop clients like OpenClaw and Hermes, allowing you to download the AI models of your choice in a fairly simple graphical UI. I tested various models in different size ranges. Asus recommends starting with Qwen 27B, a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model that splits the difference between size and efficiency. I also loaded a few versions of Google’s Gemma open models in the same size range.

It has been revealed that but these are all small enough that you could run them on a high-end GPU. To push the Spark, I grabbed a few larger models like the Qwen Flash Next, a 90GB download with 125 billion parameters. This model occupies almost all the shared memory when active, whereas the smaller ones won’t even go beyond the GPU’s reserved 64GB.

Recent findings suggest that the nice (and scary) thing about setting up a local agent on Windows is that it can control the PC. Once the model is loaded in your preferred AI framework, you can just ask it to handle additional configuration. Need to set up access for your online accounts? Just ask. Manage installed tools and apps? Just ask. Surely nothing could go wrong, right?

Recent findings suggest that in short order, I set up agent workflows to access and analyze data from test email accounts, manage local files, update a coding project, and analyze the content of images in my photo library. I also used ComfyUI workflows to generate images and videos locally without worrying about running through a limited allotment of tokens in the cloud. I’ll admit, I don’t have much use for media generation, but some of these local image models have gotten surprisingly good. Of course, the machine itself is expensive enough that you could pay for the most extravagant AI plans for a few years before breaking even. Still, the data and compute are all yours.

Sources indicate that A few tragic tales about local agents nuking file directories or exposing data have made the rounds, and that’s a real concern when you start giving these things access to your PC—these models can do whatever you can do while sitting at the keyboard. I tested the P16’s AI capabilities with that in mind, ensuring I had no irreplaceable or sensitive data on the machine. Agents are supposed to seek authorization before taking action, but mistakes may happen, even if you’re being careful.

In a recent development, the agents didn’t make any huge mistakes in my testing, but watching the chain of thought bounce around can be maddening, like an unguided robot vacuum bouncing into walls. But like a vacuum, today’s AI agents usually get to the right place.

Sometimes, it does feel very futuristic. You give the machine a problem or tell it to troubleshoot something, and it does it without sharing any data with anyone. It’s a different way of using a PC. That’s cool, but it’s also not without frustration. Even though these models are often able to arrive at the correct result, they may not do so very rapidly.

During normal operation, the Asus ProArt P16 is whisper-quiet. As soon as you start running inference for AI, though, the fans kick into high gear. The machine absolutely burns through the enormous 100 Wh battery, which is the largest cell you can legally bring on an airplane in the US. You really only get about two hours of inference without the power cable, and you might not get as much done as you’d think in that time. For example, scanning a day’s emails and generating action items takes around five minutes with a mid-weight model.

Recent findings suggest that with simple tasks, models like Qwen 27B can churn through 20 or so tokens per second (with default “medium” effort mode). That’s a bit slower than you’ll get with cloud-based frontier models, which are also more capable thanks to their powerful server hardware. As long as you don’t need to ask it if Taiwan is a country, Qwen seems like the best option for local AI currently. Google’s mid-weight Gemma models can occasionally hit up to 40 tokens per second, but that figure tends to come down to a quarter of that speed for more complex tasks.

It has been revealed that while Qwen Flash Next does produce better results, it takes so long I usually stick with the smaller models—it chugs along at just a few tokens per second unless you drop its thinking level. You can still make use of all that RAM by running multiple concurrent agents, though. That may be the real promise of RTX Spark machines, but that requires you to have a lot of AI-powered projects in mind. If you’re just using a Spark laptop as an alternative to keeping a ChatGPT window open, you should probably pay for ChatGPT Pro instead of buying a $7,000 PC.

In a recent development, while the RTX Spark is aimed at AI workloads, it’s also an all-around speedy Windows platform. It is, however, an Arm-based chip with 20 Nvidia Grace CPU cores. Microsoft has a sordid history with Windows on Arm, but things are finally in a better place.

It has been revealed that the Windows Prism emulator can run x86 and x64 programs well enough that you won’t usually notice the difference, and some past software gaps, like Google Drive and VPN apps, have been addressed with native Arm versions. So you don’t need to fear Arm chips on Windows anymore unless you have very specific legacy software and hardware needs.

In daily use, the ProArt P16 with RTX Spark is extremely responsive. It’s still usable even when you fill up the memory with AI agents running inference in the background. There are very few systems that directly compare to the RTX Spark right now, but here are some system benchmarks of the Asus ProArt P16.

Nvidia has pushed the idea that Spark can be your primary gaming machine, too. But here, emulation is more of a bother. There are virtually no native Arm games for Windows, and emulation takes a bite out of your performance. Titles that require system-level anti-cheat measures may not run because those cannot be emulated. However, Nvidia has made progress here, collaborating with some major vendors like Easy Anti-Cheat, BattlEye, and Denuvo to support their technology on Spark. It’s still early, though, and you may encounter errors.

Sources indicate that the GPU component of the Spark N1X is equivalent to the most powerful Blackwell-based gaming GPUs on the market, but emulation means performance won’t quite measure up. You also have to remember that the ProArt P16 has an incredibly high-resolution OLED screen. Running games at native resolution, even without the emulation overhead, is already pushing the limits of the hardware.

Recent findings suggest that aside from the benchmark numbers, I put the ProArt P16 to work playing some games. While they ran well enough to play, it’s not as simple as cranking the settings to max like you would on an x86 system with a Blackwell GPU. For example, Baldur’s Gate 3 is not exactly a graphical tour de force, and it’s more CPU-bound than some other AAA games.

Recent findings suggest that I had to make some compromises to maintain 60 fps, even in less busy areas of the game. It was basically a trade-off between lowering detail and using aggressive DLSS or dropping the game below native resolution. You can expect Spark-based machines like this to run most games with high graphical settings, but ultra settings will be out of reach if you want to maintain good frame rates.

In a recent development, in a purely technical way, it’s cool that you can run powerful 100GB AI models on a laptop. Devices like the DGX Spark and DIY GPU clusters can perform similar tasks, but having everything centralized on one machine makes it more appealing as a way to get things done with AI, and Windows makes it easy to get started.

According to recent reports, the ProArt P16 can be your one and only computer, handling gaming, productivity, and AI inference. However, it can be hard to really take advantage of all the AI capabilities of the machine. You’re looking at running either one or two large, powerful agents at very slow speeds or a collection of smaller models much faster. That means you need to have plenty of AI applications in mind. Otherwise, you might as well get a standard laptop.

Sources indicate that you probably already know if that’s something you want. The kind of person running multiple concurrent agentic tasks using cloud systems might benefit from a PC like the ProArt P16, and in some extreme instances, they might want to spend $7,000 on the machine with 128GB of RAM. However, you could also step down to the 64GB model to save a few thousand dollars and still get some useful AI capabilities as models get more efficient.

The Asus ProArt P16 is really a niche machine. If you want something primarily for gaming, an x86 system with a discrete GPU makes more sense, and a lighter, productivity-focused laptop is better for most buyers. The ProArt P16 offers a glimpse of how a local AI-powered future could work, but it’s not a good purchase for anyone but the most fervent AI boosters right now.
